prompt: Where do the seconds that `stats.py` reports come from?

choices.text: Ollama's price list, converted into time
choices.why: Ollama has no price list.

choices.text: The number of tokens multiplied by a constant
choices.why: Tokens and seconds are recorded separately.

choices.text: The wall clock around each call
choices.why: Right: `call()` records them.

choices.text: A table of declared latencies in the harness
choices.why: Nothing is declared; they are measured.

prompt: `v1-bare`'s median call took 12.4 seconds and `v2-json`'s took 4.0. How many times longer is that? One decimal place.
`v3-examples` sends more than twice the input of `v2-json`, yet its median is only a tenth of a second slower. Why?

choices.text: Reading is one pass; the outputs were the same length
choices.why: Right: 30.6 against 30.8 tokens written.

choices.text: Ollama skips the examples when it reads the prompt
choices.why: It reads every token.

choices.text: The examples are cached on the disk between runs
choices.why: Lesson 17 measures what a cache keeps; it is not the disk.

choices.text: Longer prompts make the model write faster
choices.why: Writing speed per token does not rise.

prompt: `stats.py` printed `p95 5.0` for forty calls. What does that say?

choices.text: The average call took 5.0 seconds to finish
choices.why: That would be a mean, which it does not print.

choices.text: The slowest of the forty calls took 5.0 seconds
choices.why: That is the maximum.

choices.text: 95% of the time was spent writing
choices.why: It is a percentile of calls, not a share of time.

choices.text: 95 calls in 100 took at most 5.0 s
choices.why: Right: on forty calls, two were slower.

prompt: `cost.py` reports 4.8168 cents for forty calls of `v3-examples`. How much is one call, in cents? Five decimal places.
At the course's prices (300 cents a million input tokens, 1500 a million output tokens), what do 1000 calls cost if each reads 200 tokens and writes 40? In cents.
Why does `cost.py` multiply integers and round only once, at the end?

choices.text: Rounding twice would give a negative number
choices.why: It gives a slightly wrong one.

choices.text: Binary floats cannot hold most decimal fractions
choices.why: Right: sums of them drift.

choices.text: Integers are faster for a computer to multiply
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Prices are only published as whole numbers
choices.why: They are whole cents per million here; that is not the reason.

prompt: Output was 11% of the tokens of the `v3-examples` run. Why was it 38% of the cost?

choices.text: Ollama charges for output and not for input
choices.why: Ollama charges nothing; these are the course's prices.

choices.text: The cost includes the seconds each call took
choices.why: `cost.py` reads only tokens.

choices.text: Output costs five times as much
choices.why: Right: 1500 against 300.

choices.text: Output tokens are longer than input tokens
choices.why: A token is a token; the price differs.

prompt: The prices in `prices.json` are whole cents per ___ tokens, so tokens times price is a whole number.
hint: Read the note in the file.

prompt: `--set num_predict=20` on `v3-examples` cut the p95 from 5.0 seconds to 3.1. What happened to the replies, and why?
hint: How long was a good answer?

choices.text: All forty were cut off before they finished
choices.why: Right: a cap is not a way to ask for less.

choices.text: They became shorter and stayed valid
choices.why: They stopped mid-string.

choices.text: Only the ones that were wrong were cut
choices.why: The cap cuts any reply longer than twenty tokens.

choices.text: The model rewrote them to fit in twenty tokens
choices.why: It does not know the cap is there.

prompt: The longest good answer to `v3-examples` was 38 tokens. Where should its output cap sit?

choices.text: At 20, to save money on every reply
choices.why: That cut all forty.

choices.text: At exactly 30.6, the mean output
choices.why: Half the replies are longer than the mean.

choices.text: There should be no cap at all
choices.why: A runaway reply costs time and money.

choices.text: Above 38 tokens
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Which of these are ways the lesson gives to make calls cheaper? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Send fewer tokens
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Have fewer written
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Pay less per call by waiting, in a batch
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Raise the temperature
choices.why: That changes what is written, not its price.

prompt: Lesson 1 found `llama3.2:1b` passing 9 of 40 where `llama3.2:3b` passed 28. What would a route sending easy messages to the small model need before it shipped?

choices.text: A higher temperature for the small model
choices.why: That is not what decides a route.

choices.text: A run of the whole route, compared message by message
choices.why: Right: like any other change.

choices.text: Nothing, since easy messages cannot go wrong
choices.why: Which messages are easy is the rule being tested.

choices.text: A larger test set built from the small model's replies
choices.why: Labels come from people.

prompt: Which work suits a provider's batch interface?

choices.text: Answering a customer in a live chat
choices.why: A batch may take hours.

choices.text: Checking a password reset before it is sent
choices.why: Somebody is waiting.

choices.text: Re-sorting last year's archive overnight
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Sorting the message a customer just sent
choices.why: Somebody is waiting for that one.

prompt: Removing the examples broke nine messages and fixed one, p = 0.021. What does that p value tell you?

choices.text: A split that lopsided is unlikely by chance
choices.why: Right: the examples were doing something.

choices.text: The cheaper prompt is 2.1% worse
choices.why: p is not a size of effect.

choices.text: There is no difference between the prompts
choices.why: That would be a large p.

choices.text: The examples cost 2.1% of the tokens
choices.why: p says nothing about tokens.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer the p95 to the mean when judging latency?

choices.text: The mean cannot be computed on forty calls
choices.why: It can; it hides the tail.

choices.text: The p95 is always lower than the mean
choices.why: It is usually higher.

choices.text: Ollama reports only percentiles
choices.why: `stats.py` computes them from the run file.

choices.text: A person waiting feels the slow calls
choices.why: Right: the mean can fall while the tail rises.

prompt: From the two `cost.py` lines, how many cents a million calls did removing the examples save (120,420 against 79,582.5)?
Removing the examples left format at 39 of 40 and took urgencies from 28 to 20. What were the examples paying for?

choices.text: Nothing, since the totals are within noise
choices.why: p = 0.021 says otherwise.

choices.text: Judgement, not format
choices.why: Right: the categories and urgencies fell.

choices.text: Format, since JSON broke without them
choices.why: Format held at 39 of 40.

choices.text: Speed, since the prompt became slower
choices.why: It became faster.

items: Trade answers for money, in writing

choices.text: A run at a higher temperature
choices.why: That measures something else.

choices.text: The model's price list
choices.why: Price does not say what broke.

choices.text: The p95, and the messages the change broke
